Then \(\dfrac{n}{t}\) is an integer and, as \(t>1\), it is a proper divisor of \(n\). Moreover

\[
\frac{n}{t}>\frac{n}{p}=d,
\]

which contradicts the definition of \(d\) as the greatest proper divisor.
Hence no such divisor \(t\) exists; therefore \(p\) is the smallest divisor of \(n\) greater than \(1\).
The smallest divisor larger than \(1\) of any integer \(>1\) is always prime, so \(p\) is prime and indeed the smallest prime factor of \(n\). Consequently

\[
d=\frac{n}{p}.
\]

---

### 2. Express \(n+d\) in terms of \(p\)

\[
n+d=n+\frac{n}{p}=\frac{n}{p}(p+1)=d(p+1). \tag{1}
\]

---

### 3. Assume, for contradiction, that \(n+d\) is a power of two

Thus there exists an integer \(k\ge 1\) such that

\[
d(p+1)=2^{k}. \tag{2}
\]

We distinguish two cases.

---

#### **Case 1:** \(p=2\)

Then (2) becomes \(3d=2^{k}\). The left‑hand side is divisible by the prime \(3\), whereas a power of two has no odd prime factor – impossible. Hence this case cannot occur.

---

#### **Case 2:** \(p\) is odd

Here \(p\ge 3\); therefore \(p+1\) is even and at least \(4\).

Because the right‑hand side of (2) is a power of two, its only prime factor is \(2\). Consequently any odd prime factor of \(d\) or of \(p+1\) would also divide \(2^{k}\), which is impossible. Hence

* \(d\) has no odd prime factors. Since \(d>1\), this forces \(d=2^{a}\) for some integer \(a\ge 1\).
* \(p+1\) has no odd prime factors. As \(p+1>1\), this forces \(p+1=2^{b}\) for some integer \(b\ge 1\). Because \(p+1\) is even and \(p\ge 3\), we have \(p+1\ge 4\); thus \(b\ge 2\).

So we can write \(p=2^{b}-1\) (an odd prime) and \(d=2^{a}\) with \(a\ge 1\).

Now

\[
n=p\,d=(2^{b}-1)\cdot 2^{a}.
\]

Since \(a\ge 1\), the factor \(2^{a}\) contains the prime \(2\); therefore \(n\) is even and \(2\mid n\).

Recall that by the argument of §1, \(p\) is the **smallest** divisor of \(n\) greater than \(1\). Because \(2\) divides \(n\) and \(2>1\), the smallest such divisor cannot exceed \(2\); in fact it must be \(2\). This contradicts the fact that \(p\) is odd (\(p\ge 3\)). Hence this case is also impossible.

---

\[
\boxed{\text{For every integer }n\ge2\text{ with }d>1,\; n+d\text{ is not a power of }2.}
\]

Proof: We are given 70‑digit numbers whose decimal expansion contains each digit \(1,2,\dots ,7\) exactly ten times; digits \(8,9,0\) never occur.
Let \(n\) and \(m\) be two such numbers and assume that \(n\) divides \(m\) with \(n\neq m\). We shall derive a contradiction.

---

### 1. A congruence modulo 9

The sum of the digits of any such number is

\[
10(1+2+\cdots +7)=10\cdot28=280 .
\]

For any integer, the remainder modulo 9 equals the remainder of its digit sum modulo 9. Hence

\[
n\equiv 280\equiv 1\pmod 9,\qquad
m\equiv 1\pmod 9 .
\]

---

### 2. The quotient must be \(\equiv1\pmod9\)

Because \(n\mid m\) and \(n,m>0\), we have \(m=n\cdot k\) for some positive integer \(k\).
If \(n>m\) then \(m=n\cdot k\) would force \(k=0\) (impossible) or \(k\) negative; thus the only possibility with distinct numbers is \(n<m\) and therefore \(k\ge 2\).

Reducing \(m=nk\) modulo 9 gives

\[
1\equiv m\equiv nk\equiv 1\cdot k\equiv k\pmod 9,
\]

so \(k\equiv 1\pmod 9\).
The smallest integer \(\ge2\) that is congruent to \(1\) modulo 9 is \(10\); consequently \(k\ge 10\).

---

### 3. Size contradiction

A 70‑digit integer satisfies

\[
10^{69}\le n\le 10^{70}-1 .
\]

(The lower bound follows from the definition of a 70‑digit number.)
Multiplying by \(k\ge10\) we obtain

\[
m=nk\ge 10^{69}\cdot10 = 10^{70}.
\]

But \(m\) is also a 70‑digit number, so we must have

\[
m\le 10^{70}-1 .
\]

The two inequalities \(m\ge 10^{70}\) and \(m\le 10^{70}-1\) cannot hold simultaneously – a contradiction.

---

### 4. Conclusion

Our assumption that two distinct numbers of the described form could divide one another is impossible. Hence **no such number can divide another (different) number of the same form**. ∎

Problem: Prove that for any positive $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ and $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ the inequality

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} y_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}+y_{i}\right)^{2}}
$$

holds.

Proof: We prove the inequality

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_i y_i}\;\ge\;\frac{4n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i)^{2}}\qquad (x_i,y_i>0).
\]

---

### 1. Engel’s (Cauchy–Schwarz) form

For positive numbers \(b_i\) we have \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{a_i^{2}}{b_i}\ge\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i}\).
Take \(a_i=1,\;b_i=x_i y_i\). Then

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_i y_i}
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1^{2}}{x_i y_i}
\ge\frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}1)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}
=\frac{n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}. \tag{1}
\]

---

### 2. A simple quadratic estimate

For each \(i\),

\[
(x_i+y_i)^{2}=x_i^{2}+2x_i y_i+y_i^{2}\ge 4x_i y_i,
\]

because \((x_i-y_i)^{2}=x_i^{2}+y_i^{2}-2x_i y_i\ge0\) gives \(x_i^{2}+y_i^{2}\ge2x_i y_i\).
Summing over \(i\) yields

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i)^{2}\;\ge\;4\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i. \tag{2}
\]

All sums are positive, therefore (2) can be rewritten as

\[
\frac{1}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}\;\ge\;\frac{4}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i)^{2}}. \tag{3}
\]

Multiplying (3) by \(n^{2}\) gives

\[
\frac{n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}\;\ge\;\frac{4n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i)^{2}}. \tag{4}
\]

---

### 3. Combining the estimates

From (1) and (4) we obtain

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_i y_i}
\;\ge\; \frac{n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}
\;\ge\; \frac{4n^{2}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i+y_i)^{2}},
\]

which is exactly the required inequality.

---

### 4. Equality case

* Equality in (1) (Engel) holds iff all \(x_i y_i\) are equal (because \(a_i=1\) must be proportional to \(b_i=x_i y_i\)).
* Equality in (2) holds iff \((x_i-y_i)^{2}=0\) for every \(i\), i.e. \(x_i=y_i\) for all \(i\).

Both conditions together imply \(x_i=y_i\) and all \(x_i\) (hence all \(y_i\)) are equal. Thus equality occurs exactly when

\[
x_1=x_2=\dots =x_n = y_1 = y_2 = \dots = y_n = c>0.
\]

In that case both sides equal \(\displaystyle\frac{n}{c^{2}}\).

∎

Proof: **Solution.**

Choose the coordinate axes so that the \(x\)-axis is parallel to the chord \(AC\).
Because \(AC\) is then horizontal, it lies on a line of the form \(y=y_{0}\) for some constant \(y_{0}\).

The points \(A\) and \(C\) are on the circle and satisfy \(y=y_{0}\); hence their \(x\)-coordinates obey
\(x^{2}=R^{2}-y_{0}^{2}\). Since \(A\neq C\) (a chord has two distinct endpoints), the two values are opposite numbers. We can therefore write
\[
A=(a,y_{0}),\qquad C=(-a,y_{0})\qquad (a\neq0).
\]

Chord \(BD\) is perpendicular to \(AC\). As \(AC\) is horizontal, \(BD\) is vertical; thus \(BD\) lies on a line \(x=x_{0}\) for some constant \(x_{0}\).
Substituting \(x=x_{0}\) into the circle equation gives \(y^{2}=R^{2}-x_{0}^{2}\), so the two intersection points have opposite \(y\)-coordinates. Consequently
\[
B=(x_{0},b),\qquad D=(x_{0},-b)\qquad (b\neq0).
\]

The intersection point \(M\) of \(AC\;(y=y_{0})\) and \(BD\;(x=x_{0})\) is simply
\[
M=(x_{0},y_{0}).
\]

Now compute the midpoints:
\[
K\;(\text{midpoint of }AB)=\Bigl(\frac{a+x_{0}}{2},\frac{y_{0}+b}{2}\Bigr),\qquad
L\;(\text{midpoint of }CD)=\Bigl(\frac{-a+x_{0}}{2},\frac{y_{0}-b}{2}\Bigr).
\]

Adding these two vectors yields
\[
K+L=\Bigl(\frac{a+x_{0}-a+x_{0}}{2},\frac{y_{0}+b+y_{0}-b}{2}\Bigr)=(x_{0},y_{0})=M.
\]
Thus
\[
M=K+L\qquad(\text{and because }O\text{ is the origin, } \overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OK}+\overrightarrow{OL}).
\]

Consider the quadrilateral taken in order \(O\!\to\!K\!\to\!M\!\to\!L\!\to\!O\).
\[
\overrightarrow{OK}=K,\qquad
\overrightarrow{LM}=M-L=K=\overrightarrow{OK},
\]
so \(OK\) and \(LM\) are parallel and equal in length.

Also
\[
\overrightarrow{KM}=M-K=\Bigl(\frac{x_{0}-a}{2},\frac{y_{0}-b}{2}\Bigr),\qquad
\overrightarrow{LO}=O-L=-L=\Bigl(\frac{a-x_{0}}{2},\frac{b-y_{0}}{2}\Bigr)=-\overrightarrow{KM},
\]
hence \(LO\) is parallel to \(KM\) and \(|LO|=|KM|\).

Both pairs of opposite sides are therefore parallel and equal; consequently \(OKML\) is a parallelogram. ∎

**Solution Outline**:

1. Write \(f(x)=\frac{e^{x}}{x}=e^{x}\cdot x^{-1}\).
2. Using the Leibniz rule for the \(n\)-th derivative of a product, or directly by induction, one obtains
\[
f^{(n)}(x)=e^{x}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(-1)^{j}\,j!\,x^{-j-1}.
\]
3. Evaluate at \(x=1\):
\[
f^{(n)}(1)=e\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(-1)^{j}j! \; \equiv\; e\,S_{n}.
\]
4. Simplify \(S_{n}\):
\[
S_{n}= \sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(-1)^{j}j!
= n!\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{j}}{(n-j)!}
= n!\,(-1)^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}.
\]
5. For even order \(2n\) we have \((-1)^{2n}=1\), hence
\[
f^{(2n)}(1)=e\,(2n)!\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}.
\]

\[
\frac{f^{(2n)}(1)}{(2n)!}=e\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}.
\]

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}=e^{-1}.
\]
8. Consequently,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f^{(2n)}(1)}{(2n)!}=e\cdot e^{-1}=1.
\]

Proof: The reachable configurations correspond to the linear span (over \(\mathbb{F}_2\)) of the vectors
\(v_i = e_{i-1}+e_i+e_{i+1}\) (indices modulo \(n\)).
Let \(M\) be the matrix whose rows are these vectors; then \(\operatorname{rank}M = \dim\operatorname{span}\{v_i\}\) and the number of reachable states is \(2^{\operatorname{rank}M}\).

For \(x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\), \(Mx=0\) iff
\[
x_{i-1}+x_i+x_{i+1}=0\qquad(i=1,\dots,n,\ \text{indices mod } n). \tag{1}
\]

From (1) we obtain the recurrence \(x_{i+1}=x_{i-1}+x_i\).
Define \(T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) over \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
If \(s_i=(x_i,x_{i+1})\) then \(s_{i+1}=Ts_i\) for \(i=1,\dots,n-1\).
Because the indices are cyclic we must have \(s_{n+1}=s_1\).
But \(s_{n+1}=Ts_n = T^n s_1\); hence \(T^n s_1 = s_1\).

A direct computation gives \(T^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(T^3=I\).
Thus \(T\) has order \(3\) and \(T^n = T^{\,n\bmod 3}\).

Now we examine the fixed‑point condition \(T^n s_1 = s_1\):

* If \(n\equiv0\pmod3\) then \(T^n=I\); every \(s_1\in\mathbb{F}_2^2\) satisfies it.
Hence \(\dim\ker M = 2\).

* If \(n\equiv1\pmod3\) then \(T^n=T\); \(Ts_1=s_1\) forces \(s_1=(0,0)\).
Hence \(\dim\ker M = 0\).

* If \(n\equiv2\pmod3\) then \(T^n=T^2\); \(T^2s_1=s_1\) forces \(s_1=(0,0)\).
Hence \(\dim\ker M = 0\).

Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rank}M = n-\dim\ker M =
\begin{cases}
n-2 &\text{if } 3\mid n,\\[2mm]
n &\text{if } 3\nmid n .
\end{cases}
\]

The number of reachable configurations is \(2^{\operatorname{rank}M}\), i.e.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
2^{\,n-2} & \text{if } 3\mid n,\\[2mm]
2^{\,n} & \text{if } 3\nmid n .
\end{cases}}
\]
